newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus nationalists pledge more protests.
newsitem.headline: Belarus nationalists pledge more protests.

text.p: Nationalists in Belarus vowed on Thursday to continue street protests against hardline President Alexander Lukashenko despite suffering widespread beatings and arrests at a protest against a union treaty with Russia.
The Popular Front, the most organised of Lukashenko's opponents which claims support from 10 percent of 10 million Belarussians, forecast a big turn-out at a protest on April 26.
"All patriots must fill the streets that day. It is the only way we can express our opinion," Vyacheslav Sivchik, the front's executive secretary, told a news conference.
A similar protest drew 40,000 people on April 26 last year, the 10th anniversary of the Chernobyl nuclear disaster which affected much of Europe but Belarus worst of all.

Lukashenko, who used a landslide win at a referendum last November to shut down parliament and seize vastly wider powers, has cracked down on opponents and the mass media, drawing widespread criticism in the West especially in Washington.
An unsanctioned protest to mark the signing in Moscow by Lukashenko and Russian President Boris Yeltsin of a watered-down union treaty ended in clashes on Wednesday.

"Yesterday they beat out of me forever any doubts I had that it is impossible to reach an agreement with Lukashenko. He knows only one thing -- to beat, beat and beat," Valery Shukin, a communist member of the opposition, told reporters.
Foreign Minister Ivan Antonovich urged reporters not to attend violent protests. "I cannot give you any guarantee except to follow you and tell you not to go," he said.

He also said he could not exclude the possibility that more reporters would have their accreditations withdrawn for alleged bias after the correspondent for Russia's NTV channel was deported last month.
"The mass media is conducting a real information war aginst Belarus. Everyone repeats the same thing," he said, adding it was as if they had been paid to do so.

Official figures said 107 people were arrested at Wednesday's protest at 107, but the Popular Front said 300 were detained and 300 injured when police waded into a 1,500-strong crowd which tried to march towards the Russian embassy.
Political sources and local journalists said one protester, an elderly professor, was in serious condition in hospital with head injuries after being beaten by police.
A police spokesman told reporters eight of his men had been hurt and two were in hospital.
Despite the protests, Lukashenko said he was confident of support for the controversial union treaty.
"There is a political will on both sides. It is based on wide public support," Interfax news agency said, quoting comments by Lukashenko after he signed the treaty in Moscow.
The original document, changed in last-minute bargaining between reformers and conservatives in Moscow, would have created a single state and could have given Lukashenko a foothold in the Kremlin.
The final version kept the two states separate and left much of the rest for public discussion for six weeks.

Stanislav Shushkevich, who led Belarus when it was a parliamentary democracy and was removed in 1994 after Lukashenko came to power, said the original draft showed Lukashenko sought power in the Kremlin.
"The aim of this draft was to take power from Yeltsin under cover of integration," Shushkevich, a social democrat, told Reuters. "Yeltsin may have been sick but he didn't lose his mind."
